questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: Under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 1931, the terms included the release of prisoners and:
options: A) Permission to make salt along the coast
B) Immediate dominion status for India
C) The abolition of the salt tax throughout India
D) Separate electorates for the depressed classes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Permission to make salt along the coast
Why: The pact released prisoners and allowed salt manufacture along the coast. Gandhi then went to the Second Round Table Conference.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) were not granted. (D) was Ambedkar's demand, not part of the pact.
Key point: Radical nationalists criticised the pact because it did not secure a commitment to independence.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: The vachanas, the compositions of Basavanna and other Virashaiva saints, were composed in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Kannada
Why: The vachanas were composed in Kannada, the language of the region where the movement began.
Why not the others: (A) Tamil was the language of the Alvars and Nayanars. (B) and (C) are not the language of the vachanas.
Key point: Using the people's language helped bhakti reach ordinary men and women.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: The leader whom Gandhi regarded as his political mentor, and who advised him to travel around India for a year, was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Why: Gokhale was Gandhi's political mentor and advised him to spend a year travelling through British India.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) were Radicals, and (D) was another Congress leader. None was his mentor.
Key point: Gokhale was one of the Moderates, who believed in gradual reform.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: In the royal centre at Vijayanagara, the structure called the "king's palace" is notable because it:
options: A) Is the largest enclosure, though its use as a palace is unproven
B) Has an inscription naming Krishnadeva Raya as its builder
C) Is the only building made entirely of wood
D) Lies in the sacred centre, next to the Virupaksha temple
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Is the largest enclosure, though its use as a palace is unproven
Why: The "king's palace" is the largest of the enclosures, but no definite evidence shows that it was a royal residence.
Why not the others: (B) There is no such inscription. (C) It is not of wood. (D) It lies in the royal centre.
Key point: Many names given to the buildings at Hampi come from later visitors, not from the builders.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Separate electorates
(B) Joint electorates
(C) Reserved seats
(D) Universal adult franchise

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Members of a community alone elect their representatives
(II) The right of every adult citizen to vote
(III) All voters elect representatives together
(IV) Seats kept for a group within a common electorate
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Under separate electorates a community elects its own representatives (I). Under joint electorates all vote together (III). Reserved seats are kept for a group within that common system (IV), and universal adult franchise gives every adult the vote (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps separate and joint electorates. (B) swaps joint electorates and reserved seats. (C) swaps reserved seats and franchise.
Key point: The Assembly rejected separate electorates but accepted reserved seats for the depressed classes.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: By c. 1800 BCE, most of the Mature Harappan sites in regions such as ____ had been abandoned.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cholistan
Why: NCERT notes that by c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned, while settlements expanded in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
Why not the others: (A) Settlements expanded there. (B) and (D) are not the regions NCERT names for abandonment.
Key point: Explanations offered for the change include climate change, deforestation, floods and shifting rivers.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: A sculpture at Sanchi showing a rural scene, with thatched huts and trees, was identified by art historians as a scene from the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Vessantara Jataka
Why: Art historians compared the sculpture with texts and identified it as a scene from the Vessantara Jataka, the story of a generous prince.
Why not the others: (B) is about a wicked king. (C) is a collection of bhikkhunis' verses. (D) is a Sri Lankan chronicle.
Key point: Reading sculpture alongside texts is one way historians interpret early Buddhist art.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question: Indo-Persian sources of the Mughal period used several terms for a peasant, such as raiyat and:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Muzarian
Why: Peasants were called raiyat (plural riaya) or muzarian, and also kisan or asami.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) refer to officials or landholders, not to peasants.
Key point: Peasants were divided into khud-kashta (resident) and pahi-kashta (non-resident) cultivators.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: Shankaradeva's teachings in Assam led to the founding of houses of recitation and prayer, known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Namghars
Why: Shankaradeva's followers set up namghars, houses for reciting and singing God's name.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are Sufi institutions. (D) Gurdwaras are Sikh places of worship.
Key point: Shankaradeva's teaching, known as the Bhagavati dharma, centred on devotion to Vishnu.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the amara-nayakas of Vijayanagara:
(A) They collected taxes and other dues from peasants, craftsmen and traders.
(B) The kings never transferred them from one place to another.
(C) They sent tribute to the king every year and appeared at the royal court with gifts.
(D) In the seventeenth century, many of them set up independent kingdoms.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false. Kings sometimes asserted control over the amara-nayakas by transferring them.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are correct. Options (A), (B) and (C) all name a true statement as incorrect.
Key point: The rise of independent nayakas hastened the collapse of central authority.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: In their proclamations, the rebels often referred to the British by a term that meant "foreigners". The term was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Firangi
Why: The rebels called the British firangis, a term for foreigners that carried contempt.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) were older Sanskrit terms. (C) A taluqdar was a landholder.
Key point: The proclamations presented the British as outsiders who threatened the faith and customs of the people.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: The Buddha, who belonged to the Sakya gana, was originally named:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Siddhartha
Why: The Buddha was named Siddhartha, and he belonged to the Sakya clan.
Why not the others: (A) Vardhamana was Mahavira's name. (C) Ananda and (D) Sariputta were his disciples.
Key point: Siddhartha left the comforts of the palace to seek a solution to suffering.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Harshavardhana rules in north India
(B) Prabhavati Gupta makes a land grant
(C) Bimbisara rules Magadha
(D) Mahapadma Nanda rules Magadha
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: Bimbisara ruled Magadha in the sixth century BCE, and Mahapadma Nanda in the fourth century BCE. Prabhavati Gupta's grant dates to around the late fourth or fifth century CE, and Harsha ruled in the seventh century CE.
Why not the others: (A) puts the Nanda before Bimbisara. (C) puts Prabhavati before the Nanda. (D) puts Harsha before Prabhavati.
Key point: Magadha's rise, under rulers such as Bimbisara and the Nandas, paved the way for the Mauryan empire.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Site)
(A) Rakhigarhi
(B) Kalibangan
(C) Harappa
(D) Dholavira

List-II (Present-day location)
(I) Punjab, Pakistan
(II) Rajasthan
(III) The Rann of Kutch, Gujarat
(IV) Haryana
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Rakhigarhi is in Haryana (IV), Kalibangan in Rajasthan (II), Harappa in Punjab, Pakistan (I), and Dholavira in the Rann of Kutch (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan. (B) swaps Kalibangan and Harappa. (D) swaps Harappa and Dholavira.
Key point: Harappan sites spread from Afghanistan to Gujarat, a very large area for a single culture.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.sub_topic: Chronology of the Mahabharata and its study
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) B.B. Lal excavates at Hastinapura
(B) The critical edition of the Mahabharata is completed
(C) The Mahabharata takes shape as a text
(D) Work begins on the critical edition under V.S. Sukthankar
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: The text took shape over about a thousand years from c. 500 BCE. The critical edition began in 1919, Hastinapura was excavated in 1951–52, and the edition was completed in 1966, after 47 years.
Why not the others: (A) puts the critical edition before the text. (B) puts Hastinapura before the edition began. (D) puts the completion before the excavation.
Key point: Archaeology and textual study each add something to our understanding of the epic.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question: While moving the Objectives Resolution, Nehru looked back to earlier moments in the history of democracy. He referred in particular to the:
options: B) Glorious Revolution and the Magna Carta
D) Meiji Restoration and the unification of Italy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) American and French revolutions
Why: Nehru referred to the American and French revolutions, while insisting that India would shape its own constitution.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not the examples he chose.
Key point: Nehru argued that the Constitution should borrow ideas but adapt them to India's needs.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.sub_topic: Travellers and their patrons or settings
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Traveller)
(A) Al-Biruni
(B) Ibn Battuta
(C) François Bernier
(D) Antonio Monserrate

List-II (Connection)
(I) Physician to the Mughal prince Dara Shukoh
(II) A Jesuit priest who visited Akbar's court
(III) Taken to Ghazni by Sultan Mahmud
(IV) Served Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq in Delhi
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Al-Biruni was taken to Ghazni by Mahmud (III). Ibn Battuta served Muhammad bin Tughlaq (IV). Bernier was Dara Shukoh's physician (I), and Monserrate a Jesuit at Akbar's court (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps al-Biruni and Ibn Battuta. (C) swaps Ibn Battuta and Bernier. (D) swaps Bernier and Monserrate.
Key point: A traveller's patrons and setting shaped what he saw and how he wrote about it.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Lineage)
(A) Shungas and Kanvas
(B) Mauryas
(C) Shakas
(D) Kurus

List-II (Description)
(I) Brahmanas, who succeeded the Mauryas
(II) Regarded by the Brahmanas as mlechchhas, or outsiders
(III) The ruling lineage of the Kauravas and Pandavas
(IV) Described in some Brahmanical texts as of "low" origin
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: The Shungas and Kanvas were Brahmanas (I). Some Brahmanical texts called the Mauryas of "low" origin (IV). The Shakas were seen as mlechchhas (II), and the Kurus were the epic's ruling lineage (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the Shungas and the Mauryas. (C) swaps the Mauryas and the Shakas. (D) swaps the Shakas and the Kurus.
Key point: In practice, people of many origins became rulers, despite the rule that only Kshatriyas should be kings.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.sub_topic: Crops and where they were grown
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Crop)
(A) Cotton
(B) Sugarcane
(C) Maize
(D) Tobacco

List-II (Description)
(I) Reached the Deccan first, then spread to north India in the early seventeenth century
(II) Grown over a vast area of central India and the Deccan plateau
(III) Bengal was famous for the sugar made from it
(IV) By the seventeenth century, a major crop of western India
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Cotton was grown across central India and the Deccan (II). Bengal was famous for sugar (III). Maize was a major crop of western India by the seventeenth century (IV), and tobacco reached the Deccan first (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps cotton and sugarcane. (C) swaps sugarcane and maize. (D) swaps maize and tobacco.
Key point: Cotton and sugarcane were jins-i kamil, "perfect crops", that earned the state more revenue.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: From about the sixth century CE, powerful landholders who acknowledged the overlordship of a king and often supported him with troops came to be known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Samantas
Why: Samantas were landholders who acknowledged a king's overlordship. Some grew powerful enough to claim kingship themselves.
Why not the others: (A) Gahapatis were household heads. (C) Shrenis were guilds. (D) Dhamma mahamattas were Ashoka's officers.
Key point: The rise of samantas shows the growing power of landholders in the countryside.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.sub_topic: Order of land categories in the Ain
questions.question:
Arrange the following categories of land in the *Ain-i Akbari* from the most regularly cultivated to the least:
(A) Chachar
(B) Polaj
(C) Banjar
(D) Parauti
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: Polaj was cultivated every year. Parauti was left fallow for a while, chachar for three or four years, and banjar for five years or more.
Why not the others: (A) puts parauti before polaj. (B) puts chachar before parauti. (C) puts banjar before chachar.
Key point: The demand on land that had lain fallow longer was lighter, to encourage its cultivation.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question: Impressed by his learning, Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq appointed Ibn Battuta as ____ of Delhi.
options: B) The chief of the cavalry
C) The keeper of the royal mint
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The qazi, or judge
Why: Ibn Battuta was appointed qazi, or judge, of Delhi.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) were not his posts.
Key point: In 1342 the sultan sent Ibn Battuta as his envoy to China.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Alvars and Nayanars:
(A) They composed their hymns only in Sanskrit.
(B) They came from diverse social backgrounds, including artisans and cultivators.
(C) Their tradition included women devotees, such as Karaikkal Ammaiyar.
(D) Chola rulers supported the Shaiva tradition and built magnificent Shiva temples at Chidambaram, Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B), (C) and (D) follow NCERT. The saints came from diverse groups and included women, and the Cholas built great Shiva temples.
Why not the others: (A) is false. They composed in Tamil. Options (A), (B) and (D) all include (A).
Key point: Royal patronage helped bhakti traditions spread and gain prestige.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: NCERT notes that in 1857 there were signs of planning among the sepoys. One such sign was that:
options: A) They published newspapers in every cantonment
B) Panchayats met at night in the sepoys' lines to decide together
C) They signed a written treaty with the Mughal emperor in 1856
D) They elected one single commander for all the regiments of the army
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Panchayats met at night in the sepoys' lines to decide together
Why: Sepoys held panchayats at night in their lines, where decisions were taken together.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not described in NCERT.
Key point: The sepoys lived together and shared a lifestyle, which helped them act together.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.sub_topic: A canal repaired with state support
questions.question: Irrigation works often received state support. One example from Shah Jahan's reign was the repair of the ____ canal.
options: C) Shah Nahar, in the Punjab
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Shah Nahar, in the Punjab
Why: The Shah Nahar in the Punjab was repaired in Shah Jahan's reign.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are Vijayanagara water works. (D) is not the canal NCERT names.
Key point: The Mughal state encouraged cultivation because it increased revenue.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: Kabir often used a poetic form in which everyday meanings were reversed to express the mystery of the Ultimate Reality. These sayings are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ulatbansi
Why: Kabir's ulatbansi are "upside-down" sayings, in which ordinary meanings are inverted.
Why not the others: (A) Vachanas were Virashaiva compositions. (C) The *Tevaram* is a Nayanar collection. (D) Abhangs are Marathi devotional songs.
Key point: Such sayings were meant to unsettle listeners and make them think.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: In one of his inscriptions, Ashoka expressed deep remorse over the suffering caused by his conquest of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Kalinga
Why: Ashoka expressed anguish over the suffering caused by the conquest of Kalinga, in present-day Orissa.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) were other early states, not the region he conquered with such loss of life.
Key point: After Kalinga, Ashoka turned to the spread of dhamma.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: Kautilya, or Chanakya, to whom parts of the *Arthashastra* are attributed, is traditionally believed to have been:
options: A) A Greek ambassador to Pataliputra
B) A Buddhist monk who advised Ashoka
C) The poet who composed the Prayaga prashasti
D) The minister of Chandragupta Maurya
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The minister of Chandragupta Maurya
Why: Tradition holds that Kautilya was the minister of Chandragupta Maurya.
Why not the others: (A) describes Megasthenes. (B) is not Kautilya. (C) describes Harisena.
Key point: The *Arthashastra* is a source for Mauryan administration, but it describes an ideal as much as a reality.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.sub_topic: Chronology of Vijayanagara's history and rediscovery
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Alexander Greenlaw photographs the ruins
(B) Nicolo de Conti visits Vijayanagara
(C) Hampi is declared a World Heritage Site
(D) Krishnadeva Raya builds a hall at the Virupaksha temple to mark his accession
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: Nicolo de Conti visited in the 1420s, and Krishnadeva Raya's hall marked his accession in 1509–10. Greenlaw took photographs in 1856, and Hampi became a World Heritage Site in 1986.
Why not the others: (B) puts Krishnadeva Raya before de Conti. (C) puts Greenlaw before Krishnadeva Raya. (D) puts the World Heritage listing before Greenlaw.
Key point: Hampi was recognised as a site of national importance in 1976.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Thinker)
(A) Makkhali Gosala
(B) Ajita Kesakambalin
(C) Mahavira
(D) The Buddha

List-II (Teaching)
(I) Nothing survives death; the body is broken up and nothing remains
(II) Everything is predetermined, and nobody can change the course of saṃsāra
(III) Individual agency and righteous action are the means to escape rebirth
(IV) The cycle of karma can be broken only through renunciation and penance
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Makkhali Gosala was a fatalist (II), and Ajita Kesakambalin a materialist (I). Mahavira taught that karma could be broken through renunciation (IV), and the Buddha stressed individual agency and righteous action (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Gosala and Ajita. (B) swaps Ajita and Mahavira. (C) swaps Mahavira and the Buddha.
Key point: Such debates show how lively intellectual life was in the sixth century BCE.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Harappan agriculture:
(A) Terracotta models of the plough have been found at sites in Cholistan and at Banawali.
(B) Traces of canals have been found at Shortughai in Afghanistan, but not in Punjab or Sind.
(C) Water reservoirs at Dholavira may have been used to store water for agriculture.
(D) The evidence shows that the Harappans never used the plough.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false. Plough models and the ploughed field at Kalibangan show that the plough was used.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Options (A), (C) and (D) all name a true statement as incorrect.
Key point: Irrigation was probably needed because most Harappan sites lay in semi-arid lands.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question: In the language debates, members recalled that Gandhi had wanted everyone to speak a language that was neither highly Sanskritised nor highly Persianised. That language was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Hindustani
Why: Gandhi favoured Hindustani, a blend of Hindi and Urdu spoken by many people.
Why not the others: (A) was a foreign language. (B) and (C) were the heavily Sanskritised and Persianised forms that he felt would divide people.
Key point: Gandhi saw Hindustani as a language that could bind Hindus and Muslims together.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question: Bernier described Mughal cities in a way that fitted his view of India as unlike Europe. He called them:
options: A) Free cities run by merchant guilds
B) Temple towns governed by priests
C) "Camp towns", dependent on the imperial camp
D) Port cities controlled by the Portuguese
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) "Camp towns", dependent on the imperial camp
Why: Bernier called Mughal cities "camp towns", which he thought came into being and declined with the imperial camp.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not his description.
Key point: Historians point out that there were many kinds of towns, such as manufacturing, trading and pilgrimage towns.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: Virupaksha, the chief deity of the ruling dynasty of Vijayanagara, was a form of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Shiva
Why: Virupaksha is a form of Shiva, and the kings claimed to rule on his behalf.
Why not the others: (A) Vitthala was a form of Vishnu. (C) Rama is honoured at the Hazara Rama temple. (D) is a goddess.
Key point: The sacred centre was organised around the Virupaksha temple.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Gandhi's last months:
(A) On 15 August 1947 he was not in Delhi but in Calcutta, where he undertook a 24-hour fast.
(B) He worked to restore harmony between communities in places such as Noakhali and Bihar.
(C) He presided over the Independence Day celebrations in Delhi.
(D) He was shot dead in Delhi by Nathuram Godse in January 1948.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) follow NCERT. Gandhi was in Calcutta on Independence Day, he worked for peace in Noakhali and Bihar, and Godse shot him in 1948.
Why not the others: (C) is false, because Gandhi was in Calcutta on 15 August, not in Delhi. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (C).
Key point: Gandhi spent his last months working to end communal violence.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: When the rebel sepoys reached Delhi in May 1857, they proclaimed as their leader:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Bahadur Shah Zafar
Why: The sepoys asked the aged Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, to be their leader, and he agreed.
Why not the others: (A) Nana Sahib led at Kanpur. (B) Wajid Ali Shah had been exiled to Calcutta. (D) Kunwar Singh led at Arrah.
Key point: The Mughal name gave the revolt a legitimacy that drew others in.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: The eldest of the five Pandava brothers, who staked his kingdom in the game of dice, was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Yudhishthira
Why: Yudhishthira was the eldest Pandava, and he lost his kingdom in the game of dice.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) were his younger brothers.
Key point: The game of dice led to the Pandavas' exile and, later, to the war.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: Many houses in the Lower Town at Mohenjodaro were built around:
options: A) A central temple used by the household
B) A courtyard, with rooms on all sides
C) A large stepped tank for bathing
D) A granary shared by the whole street
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A courtyard, with rooms on all sides
Why: Many houses were centred on a courtyard, with rooms on all sides. The courtyard was probably used for cooking and weaving.
Why not the others: (A) No temples have been identified. (C) The Great Bath is in the Citadel. (D) is not the house plan.
Key point: Main entrances did not give a direct view of the interior, which suggests a concern for privacy.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: One of Rani Lakshmi Bai's grievances against the Company was that it:
options: A) Refused to recognise her adopted son as heir
B) Took away the right of her soldiers to wear their caste marks
C) Forced her to accept a subsidiary alliance in 1856
D) Exiled her to Rangoon with the Mughal emperor
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Refused to recognise her adopted son as heir
Why: The Company refused to recognise her adopted son as heir after her husband's death, and Jhansi was annexed.
Why not the others: (B) is not her grievance. (C) The subsidiary alliance was imposed on Awadh earlier. (D) Bahadur Shah, not the Rani, was exiled to Rangoon.
Key point: Many rulers who lost their states to annexation joined the revolt.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Buddhist sangha:
(A) Monks and nuns lived simply, possessing only essentials such as a bowl to receive food.
(B) They depended on alms, which is why they were known as bhikkhus and bhikkhunis.
(C) Within the sangha all were regarded as equal, and members left behind their earlier social identities.
(D) The rules of the sangha were set out in the Abhidhamma Pitaka.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) follow NCERT. Members lived simply on alms, and all were treated as equal.
Why not the others: (D) is false. The rules were set out in the Vinaya Pitaka. The Abhidhamma Pitaka deals with philosophy. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: The sangha took decisions by consensus, or by vote where consensus failed.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about how the Constituent Assembly dealt with the depressed classes:
(A) Ambedkar had earlier demanded separate electorates for the depressed classes, which Gandhi opposed.
(B) The Assembly recommended that untouchability be abolished and Hindu temples be thrown open to all castes.
(C) The Assembly accepted separate electorates for the depressed classes.
(D) Seats in legislatures and jobs in government offices were to be reserved for the lowest castes.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false. The Assembly rejected separate electorates and chose reserved seats within joint electorates.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Options (B), (C) and (D) all name a true statement as incorrect.
Key point: Many members felt that social discrimination could not be ended by constitutional law alone.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question: Al-Biruni accepted much of the Brahmanical description of the caste system. However, he disapproved of:
options: A) The use of Sanskrit in religious texts
B) The worship of images in temples
C) The division of society into four groups
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The notion of pollution
Why: Al-Biruni rejected the notion of pollution, arguing that everything that becomes impure strives to regain purity.
Why not the others: (A) He learnt Sanskrit and used Sanskrit texts. (B) is not his objection here. (C) He compared the four varnas with categories in Persia.
Key point: His dependence on Brahmanical texts means his account reflects their view of society.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: To justify the varna order, Brahmanas often cited a verse from the Rigveda describing how the four varnas emerged from the body of a primeval being. This hymn is the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Purusha sukta
Why: The Purusha sukta of the Rigveda describes the four varnas coming from Purusha's body.
Why not the others: (A) is another Vedic verse. (B) is part of the Mahabharata. (D) is a later Dharmashastra.
Key point: Brahmanas claimed that the varna order was divinely ordained, which strengthened their position.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Event)
(A) Withdrawal of Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura
(B) The Congress resolves on Purna Swaraj at Lahore
(C) The Gandhi–Irwin Pact
(D) The Government of India Act

List-II (Year)
(I) 1929
(II) 1935
(III) 1931
(IV) 1922
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: Non-Cooperation was withdrawn in 1922 (IV). Purna Swaraj was resolved at Lahore in 1929 (I). The Gandhi–Irwin Pact came in 1931 (III), and the Government of India Act in 1935 (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Chauri Chaura and Lahore. (B) swaps Lahore and the pact. (D) swaps the pact and the Act.
Key point: The movement passed through phases of mass struggle and negotiation.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question: Structures interpreted as fire altars, which suggest ritual practices, have been found at:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Kalibangan and Lothal
Why: Fire altars have been found at Kalibangan and Lothal.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not the sites where fire altars were reported.
Key point: Archaeologists often label objects ritual when they cannot find another obvious use, so such readings are uncertain.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.sub_topic: When the Damin-i-Koh was marked out
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

The Santhals began coming into Bengal around the 1780s. Zamindars hired them to reclaim land and extend cultivation, and British officials soon saw them as ideal settlers. The Paharias of the Rajmahal hills had refused to give up shifting cultivation and their forest life, but the Santhals were skilled at clearing forest and ploughing the land. They were invited to settle in the foothills.

By 1832 a large area had been marked out as the Damin-i-Koh, the land of the Santhals. They were to live within its boundaries, use the plough and become settled cultivators. The settlements grew quickly. The number of Santhal villages rose from 40 in 1838 to 1,473 by 1851, and their population went up from about 3,000 to over 82,000. As cultivation spread, the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills, on to drier and rockier land.

The Santhals soon found that the land they had cleared was slipping out of their hands. The state levied heavy taxes, moneylenders charged high rates of interest and took over land when debts went unpaid, and zamindars asserted control over the area. In 1855–56 the Santhals rose in revolt. After the revolt was suppressed, the British carved out a separate district, the Santhal Pargana, and laid down special laws for it.

Question: According to the passage, the large area known as the Damin-i-Koh had been marked out for the Santhals by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1832
Why: The passage says that by 1832 a large area had been marked out as the Damin-i-Koh.
Why not the others: (A) The 1780s were when the Santhals began coming into Bengal. (B) 1793 is the year of the Permanent Settlement. (D) The revolt began in 1855.
Key point: The boundaries of the Damin-i-Koh tied the Santhals to settled plough agriculture.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.sub_topic: Why the British favoured the Santhals
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Why did British officials prefer the Santhals to the Paharias as settlers in the foothills?
options: A) Santhals cleared and ploughed land; Paharias kept to shifting cultivation
B) The Santhals had agreed to pay no revenue at all to the Company
C) The Paharias had already become settled cultivators and did not need more land
D) The Santhals were soldiers whom the Company wanted to keep near its forts
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Santhals cleared and ploughed land; Paharias kept to shifting cultivation
Why: The passage says the Paharias refused to give up shifting cultivation, but the Santhals cleared forest and ploughed the land.
Why not the others: (B) The state later levied heavy taxes. (C) contradicts the passage. (D) is not mentioned.
Key point: The British wanted settled cultivators who would pay revenue and extend agriculture.

Question: According to the passage, how did the number of Santhal villages change between 1838 and 1851?
options: B) It stayed at about 3,000 throughout
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It rose from 40 to 1,473
Why: The passage says the number of villages rose from 40 in 1838 to 1,473 by 1851.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the change. (B) and (C) confuse the village figures with the population figures, which rose from about 3,000 to over 82,000.
Key point: Rapid settlement expanded cultivation and the Company's revenue.

Question: Which of the following does the passage give as reasons for the Santhals' revolt in 1855–56?
options: A) The British banned the use of the plough in the Damin-i-Koh
B) Heavy taxes, moneylenders' high interest and zamindars' control
C) The Paharias attacked and occupied all the Santhal villages
D) The Company refused to let any more Santhals enter Bengal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Heavy taxes, moneylenders' high interest and zamindars' control
Why: The passage lists heavy taxes, moneylenders' high interest and seizure of land, and zamindars asserting control.
Why not the others: (A) The British encouraged the plough. (C) and (D) are not in the passage.
Key point: The Santhals saw their newly cleared land slipping into the hands of outsiders.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.sub_topic: Effect of settlement on the Paharias
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

The Santhals began coming into Bengal around the 1780s. Zamindars hired them to reclaim land and extend cultivation, and British officials soon saw them as ideal settlers. The Paharias of the Rajmahal hills had refused to give up shifting cultivation and their forest life, but the Santhals were skilled at clearing forest and ploughing the land. They were invited to settle in the foothills.

By 1832 a large area had been marked out as the Damin-i-Koh, the land of the Santhals. They were to live within its boundaries, use the plough and become settled cultivators. The settlements grew quickly. The number of Santhal villages rose from 40 in 1838 to 1,473 by 1851, and their population went up from about 3,000 to over 82,000. As cultivation spread, the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills, on to drier and rockier land.

The state levied heavy taxes, moneylenders charged high rates of interest and took over land when debts went unpaid, and zamindars asserted control over the area. In 1855–56 the Santhals rose in revolt. After the revolt was suppressed, the British carved out a separate district, the Santhal Pargana, and laid down special laws for it.

Question: What does the passage suggest happened to the Paharias as the Santhals settled?
options: A) They gained from the Santhals' arrival, because they took up plough cultivation
B) They moved into the Damin-i-Koh and shared it equally with the Santhals
C) Santhal cultivation pushed them on to poorer land, harming their way of life
D) The British gave them the Santhal Pargana as compensation after 1856
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Santhal cultivation pushed them on to poorer land, harming their way of life
Why: The passage says the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills, on to drier and rockier land, as Santhal cultivation spread.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) contradict the passage. (D) The Santhal Pargana was created for the Santhals.
Key point: The expansion of settled agriculture changed relations between the two communities and with the forest.
